periods.section_title: Bibha Chowdhuri — The Beam of Light that Lit the Path for Women in Indian Science
periods.activity_title: Activating Prior Knowledge and Reading the Profile

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.233): paired word-web activity — qualities of a scientist.
Let us discuss (p.237): arrange key life events of Bibha Chowdhuri in order.

time_bands.activity: Pose the opening question from “Let us read” (p.233): students work in pairs to brainstorm qualities of a scientist and fill the word web on the board. Take three or four pairs’ contributions and build a shared class web.

Read the profile of Bibha Chowdhuri aloud — teacher reads the opening sections while students follow in their books (p.232–244). Pause at key turning points (Bose Institute, Manchester, TIFR) for brief comprehension checks.

Students individually sequence the six life events from “Let us discuss” (p.237) and then compare answers with a neighbour. Take up the correct order as a class and invite students to justify each placement with a line from the text.
Close with a brief whole-class reflection: ask students what surprised them most about Bibha’s journey from Kolkata to Manchester and back to India.

periods.teacher_notes: The word-web opener primes students to see Bibha’s qualities (persistence, curiosity, courage) in the text they read immediately after, which deepens comprehension. A common difficulty at this point is students reading the text as a list of dates rather than as a narrative of barriers overcome; pause at the Bose Institute and Manchester episodes and ask “what made this moment hard?” to shift that lens. Task 1 (pictures of women scientists) has been left unanchored and may be used as a self-study look-up activity.
materials: Class copies of the textbook, p.232–244
Blackboard or chart paper for shared word web

periods.section_title: Bibha Chowdhuri — The Beam of Light that Lit the Path for Women in Indian Science
periods.activity_title: Extract Analysis — Press Headlines and Legacy

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.237–238): Extract 1 — Manchester, Blackett, and press title.
Let us think and reflect (p.238): Extract 2 — legacy, beacon, fact-or-opinion.

homework.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.238–239): answer three short questions on Bibha as pioneer and Schrödinger’s nomination.

time_bands.activity: Write the press headline “India’s New Woman Scientist — She has an eye for Cosmic Rays” on the board. Ask students what image the headline creates and why ‘New’ might be significant.

Students read Extract 1 (p.237) silently, then work through its four questions — the significance of Blackett’s Nobel status, the MCQ on public perception, the meaning of ‘celebrated’, and the ‘eye for Cosmic Rays’ completion. Discuss each item whole-class, asking students to locate the textual evidence.

Students read Extract 2 (p.238) and work through its four questions — the MCQ on challenges today, the meaning of ‘legacy lives on’, the beacon/beam metaphor, and the fact-or-opinion identification. Emphasise the distinction between a verifiable fact and an interpretive statement.
Whole-class consolidation: ask students to choose one word that describes Bibha’s contribution and defend their choice using specific details from either extract.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the full profile in the previous sitting, students now zoom in on two carefully chosen extracts; the critical-reading method asks them to attend to author intent and possible meanings rather than just recall. A common difficulty is the fact-vs-opinion item — students may treat any positive statement as a fact; guide them to test whether the claim can be independently measured or verified. The extended ECR questions in “Let us discuss” (star-renaming, ISRO, writer’s purpose) are set as homework; in-class time is reserved for the extract analysis where teacher facilitation matters most.
materials: Class copies of the textbook, p.237–239

periods.section_title: Bibha Chowdhuri — The Beam of Light that Lit the Path for Women in Indian Science
periods.activity_title: Tech Talks Podcast — AI Across Four Segments

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.244): five MCQs on the AI podcast — healthcare to accessibility.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the podcast context: tell students they will hear a four-segment show about AI called “Tech Talks.” Read the five MCQ stems from “Let us listen” (p.244) aloud so students know what to listen for.

Read the podcast transcript aloud at a measured pace, pausing briefly between segments (Healthcare, Environmental Sustainability, Education, Accessibility). Students may take brief notes on the segment that matches each question.
Students answer the five MCQs individually. Encourage them to underline the key word in each stem before selecting an option.

Read the transcript a second time. After each segment, pause and take responses for the corresponding MCQ, asking students who chose different options to explain their reasoning before confirming the correct answer.
Brief whole-class discussion: which AI application from the podcast do students think is most relevant to their own lives, and why? One or two responses only — keep it quick.

periods.teacher_notes: The transcript is read aloud rather than played from a recording; read at a natural conversational pace and use slight pauses between the four labelled segments to help students organise their listening. A common difficulty is students confusing the renewable-energy option — the correct answer is ‘improving performance’, not ‘optimising placement’ or ‘promoting alternative energy’; the second read-through gives students a chance to self-correct before the whole-class take-up.
materials: Class copies of the textbook, p.244

periods.section_title: Bibha Chowdhuri — The Beam of Light that Lit the Path for Women in Indian Science
periods.activity_title: Panel Discussion — Mobile Phones: Beneficial or Harmful?

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.244): five-role panel discussion on mobile phone impact.

time_bands.activity: Divide the class into groups of five and assign the five roles — Moderator, Principal (opposed), Teacher (partially in favour), Parent (opposed), Student (in favour). Read the role cues from “Let us speak” together and give groups time to plan two or three key points for their character.

Groups conduct their panel discussion simultaneously. The Moderator opens, gives each panellist a turn, and manages two rounds of exchange. Teacher circulates, noting strong arguments and language points for feedback.

One or two groups share a highlight moment from their discussion with the class. Teacher draws attention to effective persuasive language, turn-taking phrases, and role consistency observed during circulation.
Class reflects briefly: which role was hardest to argue for and why? Students identify one thing they would say differently if they ran the discussion again.

periods.teacher_notes: The panel-discussion format develops the formal oral skills the curriculum emphasises for the middle stage — moderating, presenting a position, responding to others, and maintaining a role. Encourage students who tend to speak with hesitation by assigning them the Moderator role, which gives structured turn-taking phrases rather than open argument. A common difficulty is all panellists speaking at once; remind groups that the Moderator controls the floor, and rehearse a simple signal (raised hand) before the discussion begins.
materials: Class copies of the textbook, p.244–245 (role cues)
Blackboard with role names and stances for reference

periods.section_title: Bibha Chowdhuri — The Beam of Light that Lit the Path for Women in Indian Science
periods.activity_title: Writing a Magazine Report on the Zonal Science Exhibition

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.245): guided report for school magazine — Science Exhibition.

time_bands.activity: Read the task brief from “Let us write” (p.245) aloud. Discuss the three format requirements — headline, reporter’s name, three paragraphs — and the conventions of past tense, passive voice, and third person. Write one example sentence in active voice on the board and convert it to passive together.

Model the headline and the opening paragraph on the board using the provided cues (organiser, date, venue, purpose, participants). Students copy the structure as a scaffold and then write their own opening paragraph.

Students draft the remaining two paragraphs independently, drawing on the cues (competitions, Chief Guest, winning team, observations). Teacher circulates, prompting students who are stuck with a question: “What did the Chief Guest say?” or “How would you describe the winning model?”
Paired peer review: partners swap drafts and check for consistent tense, passive voice use, and formal third-person register. Each partner offers one specific suggestion for improvement.

Two or three students read their headlines and opening sentences aloud. Class offers one-word feedback (clear, formal, vivid) and teacher highlights one strong passive-voice construction from what was shared.

periods.teacher_notes: Report writing for a school magazine is a functional writing form — the format (headline, reporter’s byline, paragraphed body) is as important as content, so the guided scaffold at the start prevents students from writing free-form summaries instead of reports. A common difficulty is slipping into first person or active voice mid-draft; the peer review step specifically targets this and gives students a concrete checking task. Students who finish early may attempt a subheading for each paragraph as an extension.
materials: Class copies of the textbook, p.245 (task cues)
Blackboard for modelled sentence and format scaffold
Lined writing paper or exercise books

periods.section_title: Bibha Chowdhuri — The Beam of Light that Lit the Path for Women in Indian Science

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.239): crossword — eight antonyms from chapter vocabulary.
Let us learn (p.240): suffix -ship/-ment/-hood word-building — eight words.
Let us learn (p.242): complete news report using passive forms of six verbs.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.243): Chandrayaan passage — choose correct passive form for five blanks.

time_bands.activity: Students complete the antonym crossword from “Let us learn” (p.239) individually, then check across and down answers in pairs. Take up answers whole-class, asking students to use each antonym in a sentence drawn from the chapter context (e.g., ‘effortless’ vs ‘arduous’).

Read the word-building explanation on suffixes -ship, -ment, and -hood (p.240). Students complete the eight words individually, then share. Briefly note how ‘professorship’ and ‘mentorship’ appear in the Bibha Chowdhuri text itself.

Introduce or review the active-to-passive transformation using the board sentence from the profile text. Students complete the six-blank news report (p.242) using the passive forms of the given verbs, then compare with a partner before whole-class take-up.
Quick-fire consolidation: teacher reads an active sentence drawn from the chapter; students call out the passive version. Two or three rounds only to close the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: All three tasks are anchored in the chapter’s own vocabulary and grammar context — antonyms from the informational text, suffixes modelled on ‘professorship’ and ‘mentorship’, and passive voice as it appears in scientific writing — so language learning stays connected to the reading rather than becoming an abstract exercise. A common difficulty with the passive news report is students choosing the wrong tense form (present passive vs past passive); direct their attention to the time signals in each sentence before they fill in the blank. Tasks on matching chapter vocabulary (physicists, pioneers, etc.) and the acronym grid (p.241) are available as self-study tasks for students who finish early.
materials: Class copies of the textbook, p.239–242

periods.section_title: Bibha Chowdhuri — The Beam of Light that Lit the Path for Women in Indian Science
periods.activity_title: Extending the Legacy — Women Pioneers and Modern Science Awards

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.251): read and discuss India’s new Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar science awards.
Let us explore (p.251): read about and discuss women pioneers across scientific domains in India.

time_bands.activity: Pose the framing question: “Bibha Chowdhuri received no award in her lifetime — how has India changed the way it recognises scientists?” Students share initial thoughts before any reading.

Read the “Let us explore” section on the Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar awards (p.251) together — the four categories (Vigyan Ratna, Vigyan Shri, Vigyan Yuva-SSB, Vigyan Team). Students note which category they think Bibha would have been most eligible for and why, then discuss in pairs.

Students read the brief profiles of contemporary women scientists from different scientific domains in India (p.251). In small groups, they identify one common thread across the profiles — connecting their work or challenges back to Bibha’s story. Groups report their thread to the class in one or two sentences.

Each student writes two sentences independently: one naming a woman scientist from the profiles they found most inspiring and one explaining — in their own words — how Bibha’s persistence connects to that scientist’s work. Two or three students share; teacher closes by returning to the chapter title’s metaphor of light.

periods.teacher_notes: The Bibha Chowdhuri profile ends with modern women at ISRO — this unit extends that outward to national awards and women across multiple scientific domains, making the beyond-text exploration genuinely interdisciplinary rather than a simple extension reading. A common difficulty is students treating the Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar section as a list to memorise; redirect their attention to the question of recognition and equity that the chapter raises. Task 1 (AR/VR and e-Pathshala) requires internet access and may be assigned as a self-study digital exploration if devices are available outside class.
materials: Class copies of the textbook, p.251
Optional: printed profiles of featured women scientists if available

items.source_section_title: Bibha Chowdhuri — The Beam of Light that Lit the Path for Women in Indian Science
items.source_lo: Student identifies sequence, infers authorial intent, and evaluates figurative language using an informational profile as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Bibha Chowdhuri's life chronology, Manchester press headline, Extract 1 and Extract 2 on her legacy and beacon metaphor.
items.item_stem:
Read the following events from Bibha Chowdhuri's life and select the option that places them in the correct chronological order.

(1) She joined the Bose Institute in Kolkata.
(2) She was nominated for a Nobel Prize by Erwin Schrödinger.
(3) She became the first woman faculty member at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research.
(4) The International Astronomical Union renamed star HD 86081 as 'Bibha'.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Students who choose this place the Nobel nomination before the Bose Institute years, confusing early career with the Manchester period.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Students who choose this correctly place the Bose Institute first but move her TIFR appointment before the Nobel nomination, misreading the 1949 return date.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Students who choose this omit the Bose Institute phase entirely from the sequence, suggesting they missed her pre-Manchester career.

items.source_section_title: Bibha Chowdhuri — The Beam of Light that Lit the Path for Women in Indian Science
items.source_lo: Student identifies sequence, infers authorial intent, and evaluates figurative language using an informational profile as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Bibha Chowdhuri's life chronology, Manchester press headline, Extract 1 and Extract 2 on her legacy and beacon metaphor.
items.item_stem: The profile describes Bibha Chowdhuri as both a ‘beacon’ and a ‘beam of light.’ Analyse why the writer chose these two images to represent her contributions. In your response, explain what each image suggests about her role, and consider why the writer might have thought a single image was not enough.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: A ‘beacon’ is a fixed guiding light that helps others navigate in darkness, suggesting Bibha provided direction to women who came after her. A ‘beam of light’ implies movement and penetration — it cuts through obstacles — which reflects her breaking through gender and institutional barriers. The writer uses both because one captures her guidance to others and the other captures her active force in overcoming resistance.

items.source_section_title: Bibha Chowdhuri — The Beam of Light that Lit the Path for Women in Indian Science
items.source_lo: Student listens critically to a structured podcast and retrieves specific information across distinct thematic segments.
items.source_context: Tech Talks podcast on AI: healthcare, environmental sustainability, education, and accessibility segments.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the ‘Tech Talks’ podcast on Artificial Intelligence. Choose TRUE or FALSE for each of the following statements.

1. AI-powered robots assist in surgeries, making them more precise and less invasive.
2. AI manages water and agriculture resources by predicting natural disasters only.
3. AI helps teachers spend more time on teaching by managing administrative tasks.
4. Speech recognition and voice commands are AI features that benefit people with disabilities.

options.text: AI-powered robots assist in surgeries, making them more precise and less invasive.
AI manages water and agriculture resources by predicting natural disasters only.
AI helps teachers spend more time on teaching by managing administrative tasks.
Speech recognition and voice commands are AI features that benefit people with disabilities.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — the podcast states AI robots assist in surgeries, making them more precise and less invasive.
2. False — AI manages water and agriculture resources more efficiently, and also predicts natural disasters; the word ‘only’ makes the statement incorrect.
3. True — the podcast explicitly says AI helps teachers analyse student performance and manage administrative tasks, giving them more time to focus on teaching.
4. True — the podcast names speech recognition, text-to-speech, and voice commands as AI accessibility features.

items.source_section_title: Bibha Chowdhuri — The Beam of Light that Lit the Path for Women in Indian Science
items.source_lo: Student listens critically to a structured podcast and retrieves specific information across distinct thematic segments.
items.source_context: Tech Talks podcast on AI: healthcare, environmental sustainability, education, and accessibility segments.
items.item_stem: The podcast host, Faizy, ends Tech Talks by saying that ‘AI is a powerful force for good but we need to use it responsibly.’ Drawing on at least two of the four segments discussed in the podcast, explain what ‘using AI responsibly’ might mean in practice. Support your answer with specific details from the podcast.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Responsible use could mean ensuring AI-driven medical diagnoses are verified by human doctors before treatment decisions are made, and ensuring that AI personalised learning tools in education are monitored so they complement rather than replace teacher judgment. Students who draw on the accessibility or environmental segments and connect specific AI applications to potential risks of over-reliance or misuse should also receive credit.

items.item_stem:
The sentences below are about Bibha Chowdhuri's career, written in the active voice. Rewrite each sentence in the passive voice, keeping the meaning the same. Do not change the tense.

1. Homi J. Bhabha personally selected Bibha Chowdhuri as the first woman faculty member at TIFR.
2. Erwin Schrödinger nominated Bibha for the Nobel Prize in 1950.
3. The International Astronomical Union renamed star HD 86081 as 'Bibha' in 2019.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. Bibha Chowdhuri was personally selected by Homi J. Bhabha as the first woman faculty member at TIFR. 2. Bibha was nominated for the Nobel Prize by Erwin Schrödinger in 1950. 3. Star HD 86081 was renamed ‘Bibha’ by the International Astronomical Union in 2019.

items.source_lo: Student connects an informational text's themes to contemporary contexts by examining scientific recognition and women pioneers across domains.
items.source_context: Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar award categories; contemporary women scientists across scientific domains in India.
items.item_stem: The Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar introduced by the Government of India includes four award categories: Vigyan Ratna, Vigyan Shri, Vigyan Yuva-Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar, and Vigyan Team. Bibha Chowdhuri received no award in her lifetime. Write a short paragraph (four to five sentences) explaining which category of the Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar you believe she would have been most suited for, and why. Ground your reasons in specific details from the profile of her work.

expected_elements: Names one specific RVP category and gives a reason for the choice.
Connects the category to at least one detail from Bibha's actual work.
Acknowledges that recognition came posthumously, not in her lifetime.
Writing is in complete sentences with a clear argument.

items.source_lo: Student connects an informational text's themes to contemporary contexts by examining scientific recognition and women pioneers across domains.
items.source_context: Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar award categories; contemporary women scientists across scientific domains in India.
items.item_stem: Project task: Research one woman scientist currently working in India in any scientific domain (space, medicine, environment, or another field of your choice). Prepare a one-page profile that includes: (a) her field and current work, (b) one major challenge she has faced or is facing, and (c) a connection — in your own words — between her experience and the story of Bibha Chowdhuri. Be ready to share your profile with the class.

expected_elements: Profile is one page and covers field, work, and a challenge.
Connection to Bibha Chowdhuri is specific and in student's own words.
Sources are named or paraphrased, not copied.
Ready for oral sharing with the class.
